Aerial Wildlife Survey Report 
Wildlife Management Unit 248 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2020) 
 
Background 
Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 248 (Edmonton) is located in central Alberta within the Red Deer-North 
Saskatchewan Region. The unit is approximately 4414 km 2 and is adjacent to Elk Island National Park and 
Cooking Lake-Blackfoot Recreation Area to the east, encompasses the Edmonton International airport to the 
south, and includes all of Strathcona and Parkland Counties. The habitat is dominated by aspen parkland 
interspersed with wetlands and shallow lakes including South Cooking Lake, Big Lake, and Hastings Lake.  
 
The most recent previous aerial ungulate survey conducted in this unit used the Gasaway survey method and was 
conducted in 2012. Results of previous surveys are summarized in Tables 1-3. 
 
The objective of the survey conducted in February, 2020 was to assess the status of the ungulate population in this 
WMU by determining estimates of population size, density and age-sex composition. We also recorded 
observations of additional species of interest, including carnivores, game birds, and sensitive or species at risk.  
 
Survey Method 
From February 3-7, 2020, a strip transect survey was conducted flying north-south lines at 1.6 km (1 mile) 
intervals. The City of Edmonton was excluded from the survey area, as was the area included in the International 
airport resulting in 22% coverage (with 400 m wide survey strip) for a total survey effort of 831 km2 (2096 linear 
kms flown). Snow conditions were good and uniformly consistent throughout the unit. At each observation point, 
ungulates were counted by species, and, when possible, classified by sex and  age. 
 
Sex and age classification was determined for moose by identification of vulva patch and size differential of 
cow/calves. However, due to timing of survey with respect to antler drop in white -tailed deer, sex classification and 
distinguishing fawns from does was unreliable and is not reported here. 
 
Density was calculated for white-tailed deer, mule deer and moose following Jolly 1969 (as described in Krebs 
2014) for surveys conducted with unequal sized units without replacement because the  transect lengths varied. 
Density was multiplied by the WMU area to determine population estimates. 90% confidence intervals were also 
calculated. A correction factor of 83% for deer detectability was applied to population and density estimates (Habib 
et al. 2012), with a factor of 95% applied to moose density and population estimates. 
 
Elk observations were recorded during the survey, but population estimates were not calculated because the 
design of this survey is not appropriate for elk population calculation. 
 
Results 
There were 1292 white-tailed deer observed in 349 groups. The average white-tailed deer density was estimated at 
1.79 individuals/km2. Population was estimated at 5602 (Table 1). 
 
There were 178 mule deer observed within 26 groups. The average mule deer density was estimated at 0.24 
individuals/km2. Population was estimated at 749 (Table 2). 
 
There were 321 moose observed within 168 groups. Of the 321 moose identified, 46 (14%) were bulls, 129 (40%) 
were cows, 112 (35%) were calves and 34 (11%) were not classified. The bull:cow ratio was 0.36 and the calf:cow 
ratio was 0.87 (Table 3). The average moose density was estimated at 0.39 individuals/km 2. Population was 
estimated at 1043 (Table 3); 264 bulls, 485 cows and 294 calves.

Lastly, there were 13 elk (both on and off transect) observed within 2 groups. Of the 13 elk identified, 2 (15%) were 
bulls, 7 (54%) were cows, 4 (31%) were calves and 0 (0%) were not classified.  
 
We also observed 71 coyotes, 1 Red fox, 1 porcupine and 2 great blue heron rookeries.  These are incidental 
observations only and should not be considered minimum total counts.
